records.sourceFile: Partially constrained group variable selection to adjust for complementary unit performance in American college football - 2024.pdf

paper.citation: Skripnikov A. Partially Constrained Group Variable Selection to Adjust for Complementary Unit Performance in American College Football. Journal of Applied Statistics. 2024;51(3):606-620.
paper.abstract: This methodological application developed offense and defense ratings that adjust college-football team performance for schedule, home field, and complementary-unit effects.
paper.tldr: Complementary-unit adjustment identified plausible team interactions but did not clearly improve game prediction beyond schedule and home field. Reverse causality remains central, so the method is an analytics template rather than a causal performance model.
paper.methods: Game-level Football Bowl Subdivision data from 2009-2019 were modeled with natural cubic splines, grouped penalties, and partially constrained optimization. Models fully adjusted strength of schedule and home field, selected efficiency-based complementary features, and compared ranking and game-outcome prediction approaches.
paper.findings: Non-scoring defensive turnovers were the most consistent positive complement to offensive scoring. Defensive yards allowed per play had a nonlinear relationship with complementary offensive yardage. Schedule-plus-home-field and efficiency-complement models had similar test performance, while including any complementary total performed worse because of reverse causality.
paper.limitations: Score state and play calling make within-game variables endogenous. Efficiency measures did not eliminate reverse causality, play-by-play sequencing was unavailable, and the similar prediction errors do not establish incremental decision value.
paper.practicalImplications: When building team ratings, separate schedule, venue, unit interaction, and game-state effects and test whether added complexity improves out-of-sample decisions. Preserve transparent base models as comparators.
paper.athleteDev: Use team analytics to improve tactical understanding and unit coordination, not to assign individual blame from aggregate ratings.
paper.rtp: The model contains no individual health or rehabilitation evidence and should not influence return-to-sport clearance or medical workload decisions.

records.sourceFile: Positional comparison of countermovement jump performance in American collegiate football athletes.pdf

paper.citation: Donahue PT, Moore J, Peel SA, Oglesby L. Positional Comparison of Countermovement Jump Performance in American Collegiate Football Athletes. International Journal of Sports Science & Coaching. 2026;OnlineFirst.
paper.abstract: This cross-sectional force-platform study compared countermovement-jump performance and strategy among lineman, midskill, and skill groups in Division I football.
paper.tldr: Skill players jumped higher and faster, while linemen produced the greatest absolute momentum with longer movement phases. Position and mass change the meaning of CMJ metrics, so group values are context rather than universal standards.
paper.methods: Eighty-five Division I male players were grouped as linemen (32), midskill (29), or skill (24). Each completed three hands-restricted countermovement jumps on a 1000-Hz force platform, and force-time, phase-duration, jump-height, reactive-strength, and momentum outcomes were compared by one-way ANOVA.
paper.findings: Jump height and modified reactive-strength index were highest in skill and lowest in linemen. Linemen had the greatest body mass, takeoff momentum, peak and mean propulsive force and power, and longer braking, propulsive, and time-to-takeoff durations; countermovement depth did not differ.
paper.limitations: The single-program cross-sectional male sample used broad position groups. No longitudinal sensitivity to fatigue, adaptation, football performance, injury, or talent outcomes was tested.
paper.practicalImplications: Select CMJ variables that match the position and question: relative explosiveness, absolute momentum, and phase strategy provide different information. Monitor each athlete against a stable protocol and personal baseline.
paper.athleteDev: Explain why a lineman and skill player can express high performance through different jump profiles. Set role-relevant goals instead of rewarding jump height alone.
paper.rtp: Position norms can contextualize recovery, but they are not clearance values. Compare the athlete with preinjury data and combine force-time measures with symptoms, capacity, running, contact, and football exposure.

records.sourceFile: Poor isometric neck extension strength as a risk factor for concussion in male professional Rugby Union players.pdf

paper.citation: Farley T, Barry E, Sylvester R, De Medici A, Wilson MG. Poor Isometric Neck Extension Strength as a Risk Factor for Concussion in Male Professional Rugby Union Players. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2022;56(11):616-621.
paper.abstract: This prospective-season cohort study examined associations between multidirectional isometric neck strength and clinically diagnosed concussion in professional male rugby.
paper.tldr: Higher neck extension strength was associated with a lower concussion rate, but no other direction was significant and the study did not test whether strengthening prevents concussion. Treat neck work as one part of a wider prevention system.
paper.methods: A cohort of 225 professional male rugby players underwent isometric neck-strength testing preseason, with 179 retested midseason and 74 at season end. Clinically diagnosed concussions and match exposure were recorded, and adjusted incidence-rate models evaluated strength directions and composite scores.
paper.findings: Thirty concussions occurred in 29 players, or 13.7 per 1000 player-hours. A 10% increase in extension strength was associated with a 13% lower concussion rate (adjusted IRR 0.87, 95% CI 0.78-0.98). Other directions and composite scores were not significant, and average strength increased after preseason.
paper.limitations: The association is observational and based on 30 events. Attrition and injury or international-duty absences may bias repeated testing, residual confounding is possible, and male professional-rugby findings may not generalize.
paper.practicalImplications: Include technically sound, progressive neck extension within whole-body collision preparation while preserving tackle technique, exposure management, rule enforcement, and concussion recognition and management.
paper.athleteDev: Frame neck strength as a modifiable capacity that may help control the head during contact, not armor against concussion or permission to take unsafe contact.
paper.rtp: Neck strength can be measured after concussion or cervical injury but is not a stand-alone return-to-contact criterion. Follow the clinical concussion pathway and graded sport-specific progression.

records.sourceFile: Position-specific kinanthropometric traits of professional American football players - A study of Mexican LFA players.pdf

paper.citation: Vázquez-Villarreal LG, Carvajal-Veitía W, Guevara-Balcázar G, Maceroni C, López-Sánchez P, Castillo-Hernández MDC. Position-Specific Kinanthropometric Traits of Professional American Football Players: A Study of Mexican LFA Players. Journal of Functional Morphology and Kinesiology. 2026;11(1):109.
paper.abstract: This cross-sectional study described ISAK-standard position-specific anthropometry, body composition, somatotype, and proportionality in Mexican professional American football players.
paper.tldr: Mexican LFA players showed expected position-related morphology, especially greater size and tissue mass in linemen, but anthropometry classified position only moderately well. The profiles are descriptive, not body targets or performance determinants.
paper.methods: During the 2019-2020 seasons, 189 players across seven positions completed 26 ISAK-standard measurements. Five-way body-composition fractionation, somatotype, and proportionality were compared by position, and exploratory stepwise discriminant analysis assessed classification.
paper.findings: Offensive and defensive linemen had the greatest size and adipose, muscle, and bone mass, while wide receivers and defensive backs had lower endomorphy. Arm relaxed girth, biiliocristal breadth, and sitting height formed the exploratory discriminant model, which classified 57.7% correctly without cross-validation.
paper.limitations: The sample was league- and era-specific, excluded kickers, used anthropometric fractionation rather than imaging, and measured no performance outcome. Cross-sectional patterns and an unvalidated exploratory classifier cannot establish selection utility or causation.
paper.practicalImplications: Use the profiles as contextual references for an underrepresented league and assess health, function, speed, power, skill, and role alongside morphology. Avoid forcing athletes toward a positional body template.
paper.athleteDev: Discuss body composition in terms of health, function, and sustainable role demands. Protect athletes from unnecessary weight gain or loss driven by group averages.
paper.rtp: Morphology is not a readiness marker. Monitor clinically meaningful composition change during rehabilitation without substituting it for tissue capacity, conditioning, and football exposure.

records.sourceFile: Previous injury is associated with heigthened countermovement jump force-time asymmetries in professional soccer players.pdf

paper.citation: Hart LM, Cohen DD, Patterson SD, Springham M, Reynolds J, Read P. Previous Injury Is Associated with Heightened Countermovement Jump Force-Time Asymmetries in Professional Soccer Players. Translational Sports Medicine. 2019;2(5):250-256.
paper.abstract: This cross-sectional study compared dual-force-platform countermovement-jump asymmetry in professional male soccer players with and without previous severe lower-extremity injury.
paper.tldr: Previously injured players produced equal bilateral jump outcomes while retaining larger phase-specific force asymmetries. Outcome alone can hide strategy, but asymmetry was not tested as a prospective reinjury predictor.
paper.methods: Thirty-four professional male soccer players, 17 previously severely injured and 17 uninjured, completed three hands-on-hips countermovement jumps on synchronized force platforms. Concentric and eccentric limb contributions and bilateral performance outcomes were compared between groups.
paper.findings: Previously injured players had greater asymmetry in concentric variables with strong effects and in most eccentric variables with medium-to-large effects; eccentric deceleration impulse was the exception. Bilateral jump-performance measures did not differ between groups.
paper.limitations: The design lacked preinjury values and cannot establish direction or prospective risk. Different injuries were pooled in a small sample, mechanisms underlying force differences were not measured, and results may be soccer-specific.
paper.practicalImplications: Evaluate bilateral outcome and how each limb produces it, using phase- and variable-specific repeated measures. Investigate persistent differences rather than assuming equal jump height means equal recovery.
paper.athleteDev: Show athletes that compensation can preserve performance. Use the information to target capacity and coordination while avoiding alarm over a single asymmetry number.
paper.rtp: CMJ force-time asymmetry can complement the battery, but no universal cutoff is supported. Combine it with symptoms, strength, elastic and change-of-direction work, and progressively representative soccer exposure.

records.sourceFile: Profile of cervical endurance and peak isometric strength in elite professional male rugby players.pdf

paper.citation: Liston M, Fuller C, Dahly D, Falla D, McLoughlin R, Yeomans C, van Dyk N, Falvey E. Profile of Cervical Endurance and Peak Isometric Strength in Elite Professional Male Rugby Players. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2024;54(3):201-208.
paper.abstract: This cross-sectional study established position-specific cervical peak-strength and endurance profiles in elite professional male rugby players.
paper.tldr: Cervical strength and endurance differed by position, age, mass, and individual, with front-row forwards strongest. These are contextual norms, not concussion-protection or return-to-contact thresholds.
paper.methods: One hundred thirty-six players, grouped as front row, other forwards, or backs, completed multidirectional peak isometric tests followed by loaded flexion and extension endurance tests. Strength was normalized to body mass and regression examined demographic and position relationships.
paper.findings: Front-row forwards were strongest and backs weakest. Extension produced 429 ± 104 N and flexion 275 ± 65 N overall; flexion and extension endurance averaged 52.9 ± 20.1 and 55.7 ± 17.1 seconds. Peak flexion strength related to flexion endurance, while other forwards had lower extension endurance.
paper.limitations: Testing occurred once in preseason with varied prior training. The male professional sample may not generalize, criterion validity was unestablished, the best of three trials ignored variability, test order was fixed, and endurance termination used visual judgment.
paper.practicalImplications: Standardize cervical testing and interpret results by position, body mass, age, technique, and the athlete's repeat history. Use strength and endurance as different capacities rather than interchangeable scores.
paper.athleteDev: Build neck capacity progressively and explain why positional contact demands differ. Avoid presenting a population average as a pass-fail target.
paper.rtp: Use cervical testing as one component after head or neck injury. Clinical status, symptom-free exertion, neurologic and musculoskeletal findings, contact progression, and sport demands remain essential.

records.sourceFile: Factors Contributing to Chronic Ankle Instability- A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Systematic Reviews.pdf

paper.citation: Thompson C, Schabrun S, Romero R, Bialocerkowski A, van Dieen J, Marshall P. Factors Contributing to Chronic Ankle Instability: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Systematic Reviews. Sports Medicine. 2018;48(1):189-205.
paper.abstract: This overview of systematic reviews reanalyzed primary evidence on balance, reaction time, strength, proprioception, and other factors associated with chronic or nonspecific ankle instability.
paper.tldr: Dynamic balance, peroneal reaction time, and eversion strength were supported for nonspecific ankle instability, but most studies did not define chronic ankle instability properly. Apply a multidomain assessment without claiming one causal deficit.
paper.methods: Twelve systematic reviews were quality-rated with modified R-AMSTAR. Comparable primary studies were reanalyzed by outcome, evidence strength was synthesized, and participant criteria were checked against International Ankle Consortium recommendations.
paper.findings: Strong evidence supported dynamic-balance, peroneal-reaction-time, and eversion-strength deficits and moderate evidence proprioception and static-balance deficits in nonspecific instability. Only 17% of primary studies measured a clearly defined CAI population, substantially limiting CAI-specific inference.
paper.limitations: Definitions, inclusion criteria, outcomes, and primary studies overlapped and were heterogeneous, with wide prediction intervals. Most evidence preceded consensus criteria, and later research was not included.
paper.practicalImplications: Assess history, symptoms, recurrent giving way, dynamic and static balance, strength, reaction, range, and functional demands. Treat the pattern of deficits rather than one proposed mechanism.
paper.athleteDev: Explain that chronic ankle instability is multifactorial and trainable. Progress balance, strength, reaction, and sport tasks based on the athlete's demonstrated needs.
paper.rtp: No single balance or strength test is a clearance criterion. Confirm symptom control, multidirectional capacity, reactive tasks, confidence, and full sport exposure.

records.sourceFile: Foam rolling training effects on range of motion - A systematic review and meta-analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Konrad A, Nakamura M, Tilp M, Donti O, Behm DG. Foam Rolling Training Effects on Range of Motion: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Sports Medicine. 2022;52(10):2523-2535.
paper.abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated chronic foam-rolling effects on joint range of motion in healthy participants.
paper.tldr: Repeated foam rolling moderately improved range of motion on average, particularly beyond four weeks, but response differed by joint and muscle and did not establish a performance or injury benefit.
paper.methods: Eleven randomized or controlled studies with 290 participants and 46 effects were pooled in random-effects models. Subgroups compared intervention duration, muscle group, and study design.
paper.findings: Foam rolling favored control with an effect size of 0.823 (95% CI 0.325-1.322; p=0.001; I2=72.76%). Interventions longer than four weeks produced larger gains, and hamstring and quadriceps rolling improved ROM while triceps-surae rolling did not improve dorsiflexion.
paper.limitations: Heterogeneity was substantial and one study had an extreme effect. Dose, pressure, frequency, population, and outcome varied; only three moderators were tested, and participants were mostly young healthy adults.
paper.practicalImplications: Use repeated foam rolling when a specific ROM outcome, tolerance, and available time justify it. Measure the target joint and stop if the intervention adds burden without useful change.
paper.athleteDev: Foam rolling is an option rather than a requirement. Athletes can choose it when it helps motion or preparation while keeping strength, skill, and recovery priorities intact.
paper.rtp: ROM improvement does not demonstrate tissue capacity or sport readiness. Combine any foam-rolling response with progressive loading and functional exposure.

records.sourceFile: Got Beer - A Systematic Review of Beer and Exercise.pdf

paper.citation: Wynne JL, Wilson PB. Got Beer? A Systematic Review of Beer and Exercise. International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism. 2021;31(5):438-450.
paper.abstract: This systematic review evaluated acute and chronic beer ingestion in relation to hydration, recovery, performance, adaptation, and health outcomes around exercise.
paper.tldr: Lower-alcohol beer retained fluid better than stronger beer under controlled conditions, but evidence was small, male-dominant, and artificial. Alcoholic beer should not be recommended as recovery, and nonalcoholic-beer findings are distinct.
paper.methods: Two reviewers searched three databases and included 16 randomized or nonrandomized human experiments, 12 acute and four chronic. Outcomes included hydration, performance, soreness, muscle protein synthesis, body composition, strength, and respiratory illness; mean PEDro quality was 5.1.
paper.findings: Lower-alcohol beer generally produced less diuresis than stronger beer, and added sodium sometimes improved retention with palatability tradeoffs. One nonalcoholic polyphenol-rich beer study suggested fewer postmarathon respiratory infections. Moderate beer intake showed no clear chronic body-composition or strength effect.
paper.limitations: Samples were small and mostly male, blinding was difficult, protocols and doses varied, most hydration studies fixed drink volume and withheld food, and chronic studies lasted only four to ten weeks.
paper.practicalImplications: For recovery, prioritize nonalcoholic fluids, sodium when indicated, carbohydrate, protein, and food. If an adult athlete elects alcohol, discuss dose, fluid losses, sleep, medication, safety, policy, and timing without presenting beer as therapeutic.
paper.athleteDev: Make alcohol conversations factual and nonjudgmental. Separate social choice from recovery need and help athletes plan transport, hydration, nutrition, and next-day demands.
paper.rtp: Alcohol can impair judgment, sleep, hydration, and medication safety. It has no role as a readiness test or rehabilitation treatment and may warrant modification or avoidance during recovery.

records.sourceFile: Head, Face, and Neck Cooling for Performance - A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Stevens CJ, Borg D, Brade C, Carter S, Filingeri D, Lee J, Lim L, Mündel T, Taylor L, Tyler CJ. Head, Face, and Neck Cooling for Performance: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2025;20(6):743-763.
paper.abstract: This systematic review and multilevel meta-analysis evaluated head, face, and neck cooling for physical and cognitive performance, physiology, perception, and adverse events.
paper.tldr: Local cooling reliably improved thermal comfort but produced inconclusive performance effects and negligible core-temperature change. It can be tested as an adjunct, never as a substitute for heat-safety controls.
paper.methods: Sixty-three controlled studies with 618 participants tested 75 strategies including water-perfused devices, collars, headwear, cold air, packs, towels, menthol, and water spraying. Multilevel models pooled physical, physiological, and perceptual outcomes; cognitive outcomes were too heterogeneous to pool.
paper.findings: Self-paced and fixed-intensity performance intervals ranged from no effect to medium benefit and excluded meaningful harm. Cooling improved target-site temperature, thermal sensation, and comfort, while heart rate, core temperature, and mean skin temperature changed negligibly. Adverse events were rare and no modality was superior.
paper.limitations: Sixty-one studies had some risk-of-bias concern and two high risk. The sample was 86.6% male, cognitive evidence was sparse, and modality, dose, environment, and task varied.
paper.practicalImplications: Trial accessible, rule-compatible cooling during representative heat exposure and assess comfort and performance. Maintain acclimation, hydration, environmental monitoring, work-rest modification, and emergency action plans.
paper.athleteDev: Teach athletes that feeling cooler does not necessarily mean core temperature is lower. They must continue to report heat symptoms and follow safety plans.
paper.rtp: Cooling may improve tolerance during graded heat re-exposure, but it must not mask symptoms or accelerate return. Medical risk, environment, workload, and acclimation remain decisive.

records.sourceFile: Hydration, hyperthermia, glycogen, and recovery - Crucial factors in exercise performance - A systematic review and meta-analysis.pdf

paper.citation: López-Torres O, Rodríguez-Longobardo C, Escribano-Tabernero R, Fernández-Elías VE. Hydration, Hyperthermia, Glycogen, and Recovery: Crucial Factors in Exercise Performance—A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Nutrients. 2023;15(20):4442.
paper.abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis examined interactions among hydration, exercise heat strain, muscle glycogen use, and postexercise glycogen restoration.
paper.tldr: Hyperthermia showed a clearer adverse association with muscle glycogen than hydration status alone, while hydration estimates were highly heterogeneous. Manage heat, fluid, and carbohydrate together without assuming one universal recovery formula.
paper.methods: Eighteen studies with 158 participants were reviewed and 13 entered meta-analysis. Ten hydration comparisons and four temperature comparisons assessed muscle glycogen during exercise or recovery; PEDro ratings were fair or poor.
paper.findings: Hydration versus remaining dehydrated had a nonsignificant pooled glycogen effect (estimate 0.79, 95% CI -0.54 to 2.12; p=0.24; I2=91.88%). Higher temperature was associated with lower postexercise glycogen across four studies (estimate -1.52, 95% CI -2.52 to -0.53; p=0.003; I2=66.81%).
paper.limitations: The small, often old studies used varied heat, dehydration, exercise, biopsy, and recovery protocols and had low quality scores. Heat and dehydration were difficult to separate, and glycogen measures are mechanistic rather than direct performance outcomes.
paper.practicalImplications: Plan fluid, sodium, carbohydrate, cooling, and recovery time from environmental load, sweat losses, gastrointestinal tolerance, and the next performance demand. Verify hydration and fueling rather than relying on thirst or a fixed recipe alone.
paper.athleteDev: Teach athletes to start demanding heat sessions prepared, replace realistic losses, and pair postexercise fluid with carbohydrate and food when rapid turnaround matters.
paper.rtp: During reconditioning, heat and dehydration can amplify session strain. Progress environmental exposure deliberately and monitor symptoms, fluid balance, fueling tolerance, and next-session recovery.

records.sourceFile: Intermittent Fasting - Does it affect sports performance - A systematic review.pdf

paper.citation: Conde-Pipó J, Mora-Fernandez A, Martinez-Bebia M, Gimenez-Blasi N, Lopez-Moro A, Latorre JA, Almendros-Ruiz A, Requena B, Mariscal-Arcas M. Intermittent Fasting: Does It Affect Sports Performance? A Systematic Review. Nutrients. 2024;16(1):168.
paper.abstract: This systematic review summarized effects of intermittent fasting and time-restricted eating on athlete performance, physical capacities, and body composition.
paper.tldr: Performance was often maintained and fat mass sometimes decreased, but fasting format, calorie intake, training, sleep, hydration, and Ramadan context were too heterogeneous to claim a performance benefit.
paper.methods: Twenty-five adult-athlete or exercising-population studies published since 2013 were selected from PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus. The review summarized aerobic and anaerobic capacity, strength, power, lean and fat mass, and risk of bias without meta-analysis.
paper.findings: Most time-restricted or intermittent-fasting studies reported maintained strength and sport performance with possible fat-mass reduction and lean-mass preservation. Selected Ramadan-fasting studies showed lower aerobic test performance, reflecting combined changes in food, fluid, sleep, and activity timing.
paper.limitations: Interventions, fasting hours, calorie control, populations, tests, and outcomes varied markedly. Some studies did not measure energy intake, many were short, and caloric deficit and Ramadan-specific sleep and hydration changes confounded conclusions.
paper.practicalImplications: Use intermittent fasting only when it fits the athlete's goals, health, preference, schedule, and ability to meet energy, protein, carbohydrate, micronutrient, and fluid needs. Coordinate training and feeding with a sports dietitian.
paper.athleteDev: Avoid presenting fasting as a shortcut. Protect energy availability, sleep, recovery, and relationship with food, while respectfully planning around religious practice when applicable.
paper.rtp: Fasting should not compromise rehabilitation energy, protein distribution, hydration, medication, or session quality. Modify timing with the clinical and nutrition team when recovery demands are high.
